text.p: Resources giant the Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd (BHP) would drop the group's internal performance target of a 15 percent return on equity and instead focus on measuring itself against its peers, Managing Director John Prescott said on Monday.

"The objective of the company is to perform at a level that's in the upper 20 percent of companies against which it is appropriate to compare itself, both in terms of its ongoing performance and in terms of growth," Prescott told a media briefing.
"We're clearly in a lower period of inflation than we were when those original benchmarks were adopted," he said.
"It's to avoid a theoretical argument about what's appropriate before you understand any circumstances in the world," he said.
"It's not a lower set of targets."

Prescott would not specify which companies or sectors BHP would compare itself against at the moment, except to say that BHP had underperformed against the All Ordinaries index in the past three years. He said, however, that BHP remained committed to all of the industries in which it was currently operating.
Prescott said the previous target of greater than 15 percent return on equity was not now necessarily sensible.
He said that the new performance benchmarks meant that BHP would run its return on equity and return on capital criteria harder.
"I suspect that they need to be run more robustly and I will think impact on our choice of projects," he said.
"Also, we're going to make some robust assumptions about what's achieveable in certain areas and perhaps be more concerned about possible impact of tighter margins."
Prescott said tightness of margins was the key factor affecting BHP's performance in the last year.
"Essentially, what we're saying is that we recognised some years ago we were going into a lower inflation environment and it affected the way the business had to be operated," he said.
"That's been brought home fairly brutally and we're going to address the issue and so we will make more robust assumptions about margins and that may affect the sort of projects we do."

Prescott said this lower inflation, lower return regime might mean that its peer-linked targets would be lower than the previous 15 percent regime, but that this did not mean BHP was lowering its sights.
"If they achieve 15 percent, then we have to...this is not an attempt to go soft," he said.
He said the oil sector industry was achieving about 12 percent return on equity, while the steel industry was achieving about four or five percent.
"We'll be looking at the performance of the better companies, not some average group."
BHP's shares closed down 40 cents at A$18.92 after BHP warned about tough trading conditions in the fourth quarter and a flat performance into late 1998.
